extracted.intended_audience: patent applicants, patent attorneys, and patent examiners (U.S. practice)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for preparing the specification, drawings, oaths, fees, and claims in a U.S. patent application, with rules on form, content, and claim-drafting strategy. Focuses on statutory requirements, Patent Office rules, and practical drafting cautions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification: six required parts
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification properly consists of six parts: 1. The preamble. 2. A general statement of the nature and object of the invention. 3. A brief description of the drawings, if drawings are made. 4. A detailed description of the invention. 5. The claim or claims. 6. The signature of the applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior witness requirement was dispensed with by the Act of March 3, 1915. Place claims in the part of the specification which immediately precedes the signatures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preamble content
rubrics_metrics.description: The preamble states the name, present nationality, residence, and present post office address of the applicant; if acting as representative of an insane or deceased inventor, the preamble states that inventor's name, nationality, and residence at the time of making the invention and the capacity in which the applicant is acting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The preamble should also state the title of the invention so as to connect it by name with the petition.

rubrics_metrics.name: General statement: avoid limiting particulars
rubrics_metrics.description: The general statement of the nature and object of the invention is a convenient mode of introducing the detailed description and should be free from any particularity or limitation which, if imported into the claims by implication, might reduce the patent's coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not include particulars in the general statement that could be read into claims and unintentionally narrow claim scope below what prior art requires.

rubrics_metrics.name: Description of drawings: identify figures only
rubrics_metrics.description: The description of the drawings states what each figure is but does not state the details of the figures; those details belong in the detailed description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the drawings description only to identify views and figures; leave part-level details for the detailed description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detailed description / enablement standard
rubrics_metrics.description: The detailed description must be full enough, clear enough, concise enough, and exact enough to enable any person skilled in the art or science to make and use the invention (or to compound, perform, or identify it depending on type). If the description falls below this standard, a patent, if granted, will be void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This standard is measured against a person of ordinary and fair information and skill in the relevant art, not the most eminent experts. For designs a reference to drawing or photograph may suffice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design enablement by drawings/photographs
rubrics_metrics.description: In the case of a design, the enablement standard may be met by a reference to the drawing or photograph annexed to the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design patents can rely heavily on the disclosure in the drawings; consider including clear, complete figures and, where appropriate, descriptive text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Person skilled in the art (standard of skill)
rubrics_metrics.description: The phrase 'any person skilled in the art or science' includes persons of ordinary and fair information and skill in the relevant art or science and is not confined to the most eminent scientists or most competent experts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft descriptions to enable a practitioner of ordinary skill in the art (PHOSITA) to practice the invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference to drawings in machine descriptions
rubrics_metrics.description: In a case of a manufacture or machine, the description must make constant reference to the drawings by means of reference letters or reference numerals incorporated in the description and placed upon the face of the drawings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Numerals are preferred over letters (unlimited in number, distinguishable in sound, consistent in type). Use consistent reference numerals in drawings and description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain principle and best mode
rubrics_metrics.description: For a machine the applicant shall explain the principle thereof and the best mode in which he has contemplated applying that principle, so as to distinguish it from other inventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This requires explaining the essential distinctive characteristic and stating the mode contemplated to be best; it does not require infallibly explaining laws of nature or foreseeing ultimate optimal forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims must particularly and distinctly claim
rubrics_metrics.description: The applicant 'shall particularly point out and distinctly claim the part, improvement, or combination which he claims as his invention.' Claims should be made in that part of the specification which immediately precedes the signatures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure each claim clearly identifies the inventive subject matter and is placed properly in the specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid vague, elastic claims and unnecessary multiplication
rubrics_metrics.description: Writing claims in vague phraseology to gain 'elasticity' is improper; stretching claims to catch infringers often makes them vague and prone to invalidation. Multiplying claims unnecessarily is disapproved by the courts and can be dangerous to validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer clear, precise claim language; don't add many slightly varied claims merely to 'cover' competitors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of both generic and specific claims
rubrics_metrics.description: It is proper to make a generic claim and also a specific claim in an application for a generic invention, even where only one species is described. If later prior art reduces scope, the specific claim may remain valid while the generic may fall.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft both levels of claim scope where appropriate to preserve fallback positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claiming a whole machine vs. parts/combinations
rubrics_metrics.description: If the description sets forth an entire machine that is novel, the applicant may claim the machine co-extensively with the description, but such a claim should seldom be the only one because it can often be readily evaded. Proper practice is to claim new parts and new combinations separately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include claims directed to the whole and to specific parts/combinations to improve enforceability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrictions on later-exclusive claims for same part
rubrics_metrics.description: Once one patent or claim has been granted to an inventor on a particular part or combination as performing particular functions, no valid claim can later be granted to him on the same part or combination as performing only part of those functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coordinate claiming strategy if filing multiple related applications or patents; consider simultaneous filings for different combinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: To secure a particular part or combination, specify it
rubrics_metrics.description: To secure a particular part of a machine, a claim must specify that part; to secure a particular combination of parts, a claim must specify all those parts, and the description must explain their joint mode of operation and joint function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims should include the elements you seek to protect and the specification should explain how they work together.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim parts separately even if not independently useful
rubrics_metrics.description: A part or combination may be claimed separately though it cannot do useful work separately from the remainder of the machine, because otherwise an infringer could take the important part and avoid infringement by altering how it is adapted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider claims directed to subassemblies or key elements even if they require the machine context to function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims need not list every connecting means
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not necessary that a claim specify all the various means shown in the specification and drawings for connecting the various parts; the claim should be interpreted to include such connections of the several parts as are necessary to make them operative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not overburden claims with every conceivable connector; ensure operative connections are encompassed by claim language or equivalents doctrine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of names vs. reference numerals in claims
rubrics_metrics.description: A part may be specified by name in a claim where no other part has a similar name; where a name alone is not sufficiently specific, mention the reference letter or numeral used in the description and drawings. Use of a reference letter or numeral does not necessarily confine the claim to the exact part shown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use reference numerals to clarify what a claim element refers to, but be aware amended claims with references can have limiting effects in prosecution history contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendments by reference to drawings can limit claim breadth
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the parts of a combination that differentiate from the prior art are specified in an amended claim by reference letters or numerals, the amended claim is limited to a combination of parts having those particular characteristics; the same is true if the parts are specified by names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amending claims with specific references to drawings or parts can narrow scope—amend carefully during prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional language ('means') and equivalents
rubrics_metrics.description: Where some parts of a combination operate to give motion to others, it is proper to specify them by terms like 'means,' 'mechanism,' or 'devices' for giving that motion, except when such terms describe the essence of the invention. If used, the claim will be regarded as functional and will cover only those means shown in the patent and their equivalents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Functional claiming is permissible but will be limited to disclosed structures and equivalents under established equivalence tests; avoid generic 'means' when structure-based claiming is appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manufacture claims: one claim per patentable feature
rubrics_metrics.description: In cases where the description sets forth a manufacture, there ought to be a separate claim for each of its patentable features or at least for the article without any dispensable feature; otherwise someone can remove a dispensable feature and avoid liability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft claims to protect individual patentable features and fallback combinations without dispensable elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition claims: cover entirety and specify proportions
rubrics_metrics.description: For compositions of matter the claim should cover the composition in its entirety and should either expressly or by reference to the description specify the respective proportions of the ingredients. If some ingredients may be dispensed with and that is stated, separate claims for the residue or a single claim for indispensable ingredients are available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State proportions or ranges and optional/indispensable ingredients clearly in the specification so claims can be tailored appropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process claims: cover all necessary occurrences and no more
rubrics_metrics.description: For processes, the claim should cover all necessary occurrences in that process and no more. If it covers less it will be void for want of utility; if it covers more it can be evaded by omitting an unnecessary occurrence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List required steps clearly and avoid including superfluous steps that can be avoided by infringers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design claims: reference to drawings and 'substantially as shown'
rubrics_metrics.description: In design cases the claim may identify its subject by reference to the drawing or photograph. Where a claim ends with 'substantially as shown' that claim refers to the description as well as the drawing. A design patent may contain a claim for the entire design and other claims for independently patentable parts, but several unconnected ornaments cannot lawfully be aggregated and claimed together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use clear drawings and consider separate claims for independently patentable ornamental parts; avoid combining unrelated ornaments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signatures: full name and legibility; attestation history
rubrics_metrics.description: The signatures of the applicant must embody the full name and must be legibly written. Witnesses to drawings are not required since the 1915 amendment; historical attestation practices affected earlier filings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure applicant signatures are complete and legible; follow current procedural rules rather than pre-1915 witness requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oath formality and where it may be taken
rubrics_metrics.description: The oath is not required by statute to be in writing or recorded; it may be taken anywhere in the United States before any person authorized to administer oaths, or abroad before diplomats, consuls, notaries, judges, or magistrates authorized to administer oaths in that foreign country whose authority may be proved by a U.S. diplomatic or consular certificate. Patent Office Rule 47 implies the Commissioner requires the oath to be put into writing and attested with the official seal, though oral oath may be treated as sufficient if waived.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comply with Rule 47 and provide written, sealed oaths when possible; when abroad use authorized officials and provide proof of their authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oath content: first inventor belief and timing bars
rubrics_metrics.description: The statute requires an applicant to make oath that he verily believes himself to be the first inventor and to state his country of citizenship. The customary oath applies to what is 'described and claimed' (construed disjunctively). The Patent Office rule also requires statements of residence and that the invention has not been patented more than two years prior or been described/in public use/on sale in the U.S. or printed/patented anywhere for more than two years (with twelve-month foreign priority rules).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure oath/declara­tion statements address first-inventorship belief, residency, prior patenting/publication/use dates, and any additional special-case statements required by Rule 46.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executor/administrator oath nuances
rubrics_metrics.description: When an application is made by an executor or administrator of a deceased inventor, the statutory oath is to be varied so that it can be made by that applicant; there is uncertainty whether the executor must swear belief that the deceased believed himself to be first inventor or that the deceased in fact was first inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When filing as executor/administrator, tailor the oath to the statutory form and be cautious about statements of first-inventorship; consult counsel for edge cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affirmation may substitute for oath
rubrics_metrics.description: An affirmation in judicial form may always be substituted for any oath required by any United States statute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Religious or conscientious objectors may submit judicial affirmations where permitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fees: schedule, deadlines, and consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent Office fee due with application for process, machine, manufacture, or composition is $15, and a final fee of $20 is payable after a patent is allowed and before it is issued. Design patent fees vary by term. The final fee must be paid within six months after allowance, the patent must issue within three months after fee payment, and if the fee is not paid within six months the patent is withheld; the Commissioner has no authority to issue contrary to statute. 'Month' is to be taken as a calendar month.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pay required fees on time (application and final/issue fees); missed deadlines can render patents void or undiscoverable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawings: when required and required content
rubrics_metrics.description: Drawings are required in all cases wherein the invention admits of representation by drawings. Statute requires drawings to be signed by the applicant or his attorney-in-fact; Patent Office rules require drawings to show every feature of the invention covered by the claims and, when the invention is an improvement, to exhibit the invention disconnected from the old structure and also to show so much of the old structure as will suffice to show the connection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow Patent Office drawing rules (figures, letters/numerals, signatures). Drawings should show true positions and proportions as necessary to show the invention but need not be working drawings. Connect drawings to the specification by adjacent figure numbers and part letters/numerals incorporated into the descriptive text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historic and rule-based connections between drawings and specs
rubrics_metrics.description: Earlier statutes required 'written references' connecting drawings and specification; current Patent Office rules require connection by figures adjacent to views, letters/numerals adjacent to parts, and incorporation of those figures and letters/numerals in the descriptive part of the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure part callouts and figure numbering in drawings match the descriptive text exactly to avoid rejections or limiting amendments.
